explanation: When evidence across Key Value Areas conflicts, EBM calls for prioritizing the signal most relevant to actual customer and business value, here declining Current Value, over favorable but less directly relevant metrics. The Product Owner should inspect the cause with the team and customers and adapt the Product Backlog accordingly, consistent with Scrum's empirical pillars.

question: Under the Evidence-Based Management (EBM) Guide, which Key Value Area (KVA) most directly measures an organization's ability to quickly turn a Product Backlog item into a working feature that generates value in customers' hands?

options.text: Ability to Innovate
Time-to-Market
Unrealized Value
Current Value

explanation: The EBM Guide defines Time-to-Market as one of four Key Value Areas, measuring the organization's ability to quickly turn a Product Backlog item into a delivered capability that customers can use, distinguishing it from Current Value, Unrealized Value, and Ability to Innovate.

question: An enterprise HR software product requires customers' internal training teams to prepare materials before each new capability goes live, and stakeholders have repeatedly said unpredictable releases disrupt their change-management schedule. Which release strategy best fits this context?

options.text: A fixed scope and fixed date "big-bang" release once a year, bundling all work regardless of Sprint Review feedback, to minimize disruption.
Release on demand for every completed Product Backlog item, since Scrum always prefers releasing value as soon as it is ready regardless of stakeholder context.
A fixed release cadence, so stakeholders can plan training and communications around predictable, known release dates even though individual features may wait for the next scheduled release.
No release strategy at all; let the hosting infrastructure team decide releases independently of the Scrum Team, since release timing is an operations concern only.

explanation: Neither the Scrum Guide nor EBM prescribes a single correct release strategy; the Product Owner chooses the strategy that maximizes value in context. Here, stakeholders' dependency on scheduled training makes a predictable fixed cadence more appropriate than releasing on demand, without going to the extreme of an annual big-bang release.

question: A product has grown to require four Scrum Teams. Leadership proposes giving each team its own separate Product Backlog and its own Product Owner so that each team can move faster independently. Per the Scrum Guide (2020), what is the concern with this proposal?

options.text: Developers are not allowed to specialize across teams, so any multi-team structure violates the Scrum Guide regardless of backlog design; four teams on one product must first be merged into one large Scrum Team before a Product Owner can order their work.

The concern is only technical (merge conflicts in code), and the Scrum Guide has no position on Product Backlog structure for multiple teams, so separate backlogs, each with its own Product Owner, are acceptable as long as the teams integrate their code every Sprint.

When multiple Scrum Teams work on the same product, they should share one Product Backlog and one Product Goal, with a single Product Owner accountable for ordering that Backlog, so value and priorities remain coherent; splitting Backlogs risks duplicated work and misaligned priorities.

There is no concern; the Scrum Guide requires a separate Product Backlog and a separate Product Owner per team once a product exceeds three Scrum Teams, so that each Product Goal stays small enough for one team to deliver without any cross-team dependencies or shared priorities to negotiate.

explanation: The Scrum Guide (2020) states that when several Scrum Teams work together on one product, they should share the same Product Backlog and Product Goal, and that a single Product Owner remains accountable for the Product Backlog; splitting into separate backlogs and Product Owners risks duplicated effort and conflicting priorities that undermine coherent release forecasting.

question: A Product Owner has locked the next three releases into a fixed scope-and-date roadmap to satisfy long-term contractual commitments. As a result, the Developers report they have no slack to explore new technical approaches, run spikes, or respond to emerging opportunities uncovered in Sprint Reviews. Which EBM Key Value Area is most directly being eroded by this practice, and why?

options.text: Time-to-Market, because fixed roadmaps by definition always slow down every single release compared to an unplanned approach.
Current Value, because locking scope and date always causes immediate customer satisfaction to drop regardless of what is delivered.

Ability to Innovate, because capacity consumed entirely by fixed, pre-committed scope leaves no room to experiment, learn, or pivot in response to new information, undermining the organization's capacity to deliver new value going forward.
None of the Key Value Areas are affected, since EBM only measures value already delivered to customers, not internal team practices like technical exploration.

explanation: Ability to Innovate measures the percentage of capacity available for new work versus maintenance/technical debt/fixed obligations; a roadmap that consumes all capacity in pre-committed fixed scope and dates leaves no slack for experimentation or responding to Sprint Review learning, directly eroding this Key Value Area.

question: A B2C mobile app team can technically deploy to production multiple times per day. Adopting a release-on-demand strategy rather than a fixed release cadence would most directly support which EBM outcome, assuming quality and value criteria in the Definition of Done are still met for each release?

options.text: Improved Time-to-Market, because valuable, Done increments can reach users as soon as they are ready rather than waiting for a scheduled release window, shortening the delay between completing value and realizing it.
Elimination of the need for a Definition of Done, since releasing on demand allows the team to ship incomplete work as long as it is released quickly.
Guaranteed increase in Current Value, because any release, regardless of what it contains, always raises the value currently being delivered to customers.
Improved Ability to Innovate, because releasing more frequently automatically increases the number of new ideas the Developers generate each Sprint.

explanation: Release on demand shortens the gap between an increment being Done and reaching users, which is precisely what the Time-to-Market Key Value Area measures, provided the Definition of Done's quality bar is still respected for every release rather than being bypassed for speed.

question: A large enterprise is scaling a single product across several feature teams. Per the Scrum Guide (2020), which statement about Product Owner accountability must remain true no matter how large or complex the initiative grows?

options.text: Each feature team should maintain its own Product Backlog reflecting its own local priorities.
A Product Owner steering committee should be formed so every stakeholder group has equal say in ordering the Product Backlog.
The Product Owner role can be rotated weekly among senior business analysts to spread the workload.
The Product Owner is one person, not a committee, who remains accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team(s).

explanation: The Scrum Guide (2020) states the Product Owner is accountable for effective Product Backlog management and 'is one person, not a committee' — the organization may support the Product Owner (e.g., delegating content refinement), but it cannot dilute this single-person accountability, even at scale.

question: A Product Owner is accountable for one product, but the organization has structured work across three permanent component teams (UI, services, and data), each led by a functional manager who sets that team's priorities independently. The Product Owner cannot get a usable Increment most Sprints because the three teams' outputs rarely integrate cleanly. Which action is most consistent with the Scrum Guide's view of organizational design for agility?

options.text: Schedule additional cross-team status meetings each Sprint so the three component teams can report progress to each other and agree on hand-offs toward one integrated, usable Increment, while each functional manager keeps setting priorities independently.

Ask each functional manager to increase their team's velocity so more component work is finished before the Sprint Review, leaving the last days of every Sprint for the three teams to integrate their outputs into a done Increment for the product.

Create a separate Product Backlog for each component team so each functional manager can continue setting local priorities independently, and appoint one Scrum Master to integrate the three teams' outputs into a usable Increment each Sprint.

Advocate, using data on integration cost and cycle time, for reorganizing around cross-functional Scrum Team(s) able to independently produce a done, integrated Increment for the product, rather than leaving priority-setting with functional managers.

explanation: Component teams organized by technical layer are a well-known impediment to agility because no single team can deliver a done, valuable Increment alone; the Scrum Guide's expectation of cross-functional Developers implies the Product Owner should push for structural change, not just coordination workarounds or higher local velocity.

question: A Product Owner records every request from stakeholders and developers into the Product Backlog and orders items strictly by whoever asked most recently or most loudly, without applying any value-based prioritization. What is the most accurate characterization of this behavior, and what should change?

options.text: Ordering should instead be delegated entirely to the Developers, since they best understand technical dependencies.
This is acceptable because the Product Owner should remain a neutral scribe and let the loudest stakeholder voices naturally surface the highest-value work.
Ordering should be delegated to the Scrum Master, who is accountable for the overall health of the Scrum process.

This is the 'backlog secretary' anti-pattern; the Product Owner must actively order the Product Backlog based on evidence of value, engaging stakeholders in trade-off conversations rather than transcribing requests.

explanation: Acting purely as a passive recorder of requests — the 'backlog secretary' anti-pattern — abdicates the Product Owner's core accountability for maximizing value; the fix is to actively engage stakeholders in trade-off conversations and order the backlog based on evidence of value, not recency or volume of requests.

question: A Product Owner wants a measure reflecting the organization's Ability to Innovate, per the EBM Guide, so leadership can see whether the organization is structurally free to pursue new value or is trapped maintaining what already exists. Which of the following best serves that purpose?

options.text: Total company revenue for the fiscal year (a 'top-line growth' style measure), compared with the prior year to show whether the organization has grown enough to fund new capabilities while maintaining its existing products.
The total number of production defects reported last quarter, broken down by severity and by the component in which each defect was found, so leadership can see where product quality is weakest.
The proportion of team capacity or budget spent on new capabilities versus maintaining or supporting existing functionality (an 'installed capacity vs. innovation capacity' style measure).
The number of Scrum Teams currently working on the product, tracked each quarter as a measure of how much capacity the organization has available beyond maintaining what already exists.

explanation: Ability to Innovate is best evidenced by measures of how much organizational capacity is genuinely available for new work versus tied up sustaining existing capability (e.g., technical debt, legacy support load), rather than by output, quality, or purely financial indicators.

question: The Product Owner discovers that a mandatory legal sign-off step, owned by a department outside the Scrum Team, adds six weeks to every release regardless of change size, materially harming Time-to-Market. The Scrum Master has already raised this impediment in retrospectives for two quarters with no organizational movement. As Product Owner, what is the most appropriate additional action, consistent with the Scrum Guide (2020) and EBM Guide, to drive change here?

options.text: Quantify the business impact of the delay in value terms (e.g., lost Unrealized Value, slower Time-to-Market) and bring that evidence directly to the stakeholders or executives who can change the legal process.
Redefine the Definition of Done to exclude legal sign-off so the Increment can be called 'Done' without it.
Instruct the Development Team to bypass the legal sign-off for small changes to protect Time-to-Market, since the Product Owner owns release decisions.
Do nothing further, since removing organizational impediments outside the Scrum Team is solely the Scrum Master's accountability and the Product Owner should not get involved.

explanation: When an impediment sits outside the Scrum Team's control and the Scrum Master's process-level escalation has stalled, the Product Owner can add complementary pressure by translating the delay into quantified value terms and taking that case to the stakeholders with authority to change it — a legitimate use of the Product Owner's value-maximizing accountability, unlike bypassing compliance or gaming the Definition of Done.

question: A Product Owner manages two products competing for the same limited engineering capacity. Product A generates steady, high recurring revenue but its market is mature and growth has flattened. Product B is new, currently generates little revenue, but early signals suggest a large addressable market. Stakeholders push to shift almost all capacity to Product A because 'it already proves the ROI.' Using EBM reasoning, what should the Product Owner do?

options.text: Shift most capacity to Product A immediately, since Current Value is the most reliable Key Value Area and future potential is too speculative to fund.
Since Product A already proves value, freeze Product B's backlog entirely and reassign its Product Owner's time to Product A's roadmap.
Keep the current capacity split unchanged indefinitely so neither product's stakeholders feel deprioritized, and revisit only at the next annual budgeting cycle.

Use evidence across all four Key Value Areas — including Product B's Unrealized Value and Time-to-Market signals — to run a bounded, evaluable investment experiment in Product B, then inspect results before committing further capacity.

explanation: EBM treats the four Key Value Areas as complementary, not substitutable — chasing Current Value alone starves Unrealized Value and Ability to Innovate. The evidence-based response is to fund a bounded experiment, gather evidence, and re-inspect, rather than making an irreversible capacity shift or freezing decisions politically.

question: A Product Owner accountable for a portfolio of internal tools sets up a 'portfolio prioritization committee' made up of stakeholder representatives who vote on which features across all backlogs should be built next; the Product Owner simply enters the winning items into each Product Backlog in vote order. What is the most significant problem with this arrangement, per the Scrum Guide?

options.text: It is a violation because only Scrum Masters may facilitate prioritization discussions with stakeholders.
It violates the Scrum Guide because committees are not allowed to have any input into a Product Backlog.
It is fine as long as the committee meets during the Sprint Review so its decisions can be reviewed by the Scrum Team.
The Product Owner has effectively delegated accountability for maximizing product value to the committee's vote count, reducing the role to recording decisions rather than owning them.

explanation: The Scrum Guide places sole accountability for maximizing the value of the product with the Product Owner. Turning ordering into a stakeholder vote that is simply transcribed is the classic 'backlog secretary' anti-pattern: the Product Owner stops making value judgments and becomes an administrator of someone else's decisions.

question: A Product Owner overseeing three products for the fiscal year is asked by finance to lock in exact feature scope and delivery dates for all three so budgets can be approved for twelve months. The Product Owner knows Sprint Reviews have repeatedly generated evidence that customer needs shift every few Sprints. What is the most defensible response given the Scrum Guide and EBM?

options.text: Provide funding guidance based on the products' relative Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time-to-Market, and Ability to Innovate, propose funding horizons with checkpoints for re-inspection, and negotiate scope as a variable rather than fixing it alongside date.
Decline to provide any forecast at all, since Scrum explicitly prohibits Product Owners from discussing budgets with finance stakeholders.
Agree to the fixed scope and dates, since a firm annual plan is necessary for finance to approve any investment at all.
Offer fixed dates but leave scope flexible only for the lowest-value product, while locking scope and date for the other two to protect finance's confidence in the plan.

explanation: EBM guides investment decisions using the four Key Value Areas with periodic re-inspection rather than annual scope-and-date lock-in, and the Scrum Guide's empirical pillars argue against fixing both scope and date over a long horizon when evidence shows needs change. The professional response funds with checkpoints and treats scope as the flexible variable.

question: A newly hired Product Owner asks whether the Scrum Guide (2020) prescribes a specific structure — such as a Portfolio Backlog or Portfolio Owner role — for managing investment decisions across many products in an organization. What does the Scrum Guide actually say?

options.text: The Scrum Guide is silent on portfolio-level structures; it defines the Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, and artifacts for a single product, leaving multi-product coordination to be addressed through the organization's own practices or scaling guidance.
The Scrum Guide defines a Portfolio Backlog that sits above each product's Product Backlog and is refined during a mandatory quarterly Portfolio Review event.
The Scrum Guide defines a Portfolio Owner accountability that sits above individual Product Owners to arbitrate investment across products.
The Scrum Guide requires organizations managing more than one product to adopt the Nexus framework to remain compliant.

explanation: The Scrum Guide (2020) intentionally defines a minimal set of roles, events, and artifacts for delivering value through Scrum and does not prescribe any portfolio-level role, backlog, or event; organizations wanting explicit multi-team or multi-product structures look to complementary guidance such as the Nexus Guide or their own practices.

question: In a Nexus of four Scrum Teams, the Nexus Daily Scrum is held with representatives from each team. What is the primary purpose of this event, distinct from each team's own Daily Scrum?

options.text: To let each representative report their team's individual task status to the group so a combined burndown chart can be produced.
To reassign Developers between teams whenever one team is behind on its own Sprint Backlog.
To let the Product Owner re-order the Product Backlog based on that day's stakeholder feedback.
To inspect progress toward the Nexus Sprint Goal and identify whether cross-team integration issues or dependencies exist that need to be resolved before or during the current Sprint.

explanation: The Nexus Daily Scrum exists to surface and address integration issues and dependencies across the participating Scrum Teams so the combined work stays on track toward a single integrated, done Increment — not to serve as team-level status reporting, a resourcing mechanism, or backlog ordering.

topic: Product Value and Backlog Management at Scale
question: In the Evidence-Based Management Guide, the Key Value Area 'Unrealized Value' is best described as measuring:

options.text: The organization's capacity to deliver new capabilities that support learning and adapting based on market feedback
The value already delivered to customers by the product as it exists today
The speed at which a single idea moves from being conceived to being delivered to customers
The potential future value that could be captured if the organization better met the needs of current and future customers, relative to an ideal or total addressable market

explanation: Unrealized Value is one of EBM's four Key Value Areas and focuses on the gap between current delivered value and the total potential value obtainable by serving customer needs more fully, distinguishing it from Current Value, Time-to-Market, and Ability to Innovate.

topic: Product Value and Backlog Management at Scale
question: A Product Owner for a complex product notices velocity declining across three releases even though no new scope has been added; investigation shows rising defect rates and lengthening regression cycles caused by accumulated technical debt. Stakeholders pressure the Product Owner to keep adding new features, arguing 'customers don't pay for debt work.' Which response best aligns with EBM and Scrum guidance on maximizing value?

options.text: Continue prioritizing only customer-facing features since Ability to Innovate is an internal engineering concern outside the EBM value areas and irrelevant to backlog ordering
Escalate the decision to the Scrum Master, since the Scrum Master is accountable for technical debt trade-offs on behalf of the Product Owner
Instruct the Developers to address the technical debt entirely outside of Sprints, on their own time, since the Product Backlog should contain only customer-value items

Make the impact of technical debt visible using evidence such as declining delivery capability and rising unplanned work, then negotiate backlog capacity for debt reduction alongside features, since eroding Ability to Innovate threatens future value delivery

explanation: Declining Ability to Invnovate signals a threat to sustained value delivery. EBM encourages using such evidence to negotiate balanced backlog ordering rather than deferring entirely to feature pressure or hiding necessary work outside the Product Backlog.

topic: Product Value and Backlog Management at Scale
question: In a complex product built by three Scrum Teams, a 'PO Proxy' assigned to each team logs every stakeholder request directly into the shared Product Backlog and orders items strictly by the date the request was received, without evaluating value or consulting the accountable Product Owner. What anti-pattern does this describe?

options.text: This is a distributed-Product-Owner model explicitly recommended by the Scrum Guide for products built by more than one team

The 'backlog secretary' anti-pattern; the Product Owner remains accountable for developing and communicating the Product Goal and ordering the Product Backlog to maximize value, even if refinement tasks are delegated
This is acceptable because the Scrum Guide allows any stakeholder to directly reorder the Product Backlog according to the urgency of their own request
This is correct practice, since Product Backlog ordering should always follow first-in-first-out sequencing to ensure fairness to stakeholders

explanation: Treating the Product Backlog as a passive intake log ordered by arrival date, rather than a value-ordered artifact actively managed by the Product Owner, is the classic 'backlog secretary' anti-pattern the Scrum Guide's Product Owner accountabilities are designed to prevent.

topic: Product Value and Backlog Management at Scale
question: A Product Owner for a complex product must choose between two roughly equal-effort items competing for the same two teams' capacity next Sprint. Item X unlocks a regulatory requirement carrying a financial penalty that escalates weekly if delayed, but has modest ongoing customer value. Item Y offers high ongoing customer value with no external deadline. What is the most defensible ordering decision?

options.text: Order by whichever item the majority of Developers find more technically interesting, since motivation drives better quality regardless of order
Split both teams so each item receives half capacity in parallel to hedge against both risks equally
Order Item Y first since the Product Backlog should always be ordered strictly by long-term customer value, and regulatory penalties are a legal matter separate from Product Backlog ordering

Order Item X first: although Item Y offers higher steady-state value, Item X's cost of delay accelerates sharply over time, and containing that escalating risk protects the organization's ability to capture Item Y's value later without penalty

explanation: Cost-of-delay reasoning accounts for how the cost of not delivering an item changes over time. An item with a sharply escalating penalty can be the more defensible priority even against a higher steady-state-value item, because containing the escalating risk protects the organization's overall ability to realize future value.

topic: Product Value and Backlog Management at Scale
question: A very complex product is built by six Scrum Teams. Leadership proposes giving each team its own independent Product Backlog and its own Product Owner, each free to define value and order work purely for their own component, in order to 'move faster.' Which risk is most significant here from the Scrum Guide's perspective on Scrum applied across multiple teams?

options.text: The main risk is that six Product Owners increases payroll cost, which is a budgeting concern unrelated to Scrum

Without a shared Product Goal and coordinated ordering across the component backlogs, teams may locally optimize their own component's value while the overall product's value, which depends on integrated increments, is not maximized or may not even be usable
There is no risk as long as each team still holds its own Sprint Review, since Sprint Reviews alone guarantee integration across independently ordered component backlogs
None; the Scrum Guide explicitly requires exactly this structure of one independent Product Backlog and one Product Owner per team for any product built by more than one team

explanation: When one complex product is built by multiple teams, a shared Product Goal and coordinated ordering are needed so components integrate into value for the whole product; fully independent per-team backlogs and Product Owners risk local optimization at the expense of overall product value.

question: A newly appointed Product Owner for an internal HR tool proposes this vision statement: 'We will build software that HR wants.' Colleagues say it feels directionless. Which revised vision best reflects the qualities of a compelling product vision as taught in the PO Learning Path?

options.text: Empower every manager to complete performance reviews in under 10 minutes, freeing HR teams to focus on coaching rather than paperwork, and become the most trusted people-ops platform for mid-market companies.
Keep the original wording because a simple, generic statement avoids over-committing the team to any particular direction.
Rewrite the vision as an exhaustive list of every feature HR stakeholders have requested so far, to demonstrate responsiveness.
Copy the vision statement word-for-word from the market-leading competitor's public marketing page to ensure consistency with market expectations.

explanation: A compelling product vision is specific, outcome-focused, and differentiating rather than a vague statement, a feature list, or a borrowed competitor claim. Option A gives the team a clear future state and a reason for being, enabling better prioritization decisions than the alternatives.

question: Which statement best reflects how the Scrum.org Product Owner Learning Path frames the relationship between product vision and business model?

options.text: The business model should be redefined every Sprint to match whatever the current Sprint Goal happens to be, because the PO Learning Path treats the business model as a tactical, Sprint-level artifact that the Product Owner rewrites alongside each new Sprint Backlog.

Product vision and business model are interchangeable terms describing the same concept in Scrum; the PO Learning Path uses both names for one statement of where the product is heading, so checking coherence between them adds nothing to the Product Owner's strategic work.

The business model - how the organization creates, delivers, and captures value - must be coherent with the product vision; when the PO notices misalignment between them, it is a strategic risk worth surfacing even though the PO doesn't own overall corporate strategy.

The PO's only responsibility is fulfilling the stated vision; the business model - how the organization creates, delivers, and captures value - is exclusively a finance and sales concern with no bearing on Product Backlog ordering or on the risks the PO surfaces.

explanation: The vision describes where the product is heading, while the business model describes how the organization will create, deliver, and capture value along the way. The PO Learning Path expects the PO to notice and surface misalignment between the two, since it undermines the product's ability to realize its intended value.

question: A Product Owner benchmarks the product against three competitors and finds it lags in raw feature count, but its Net Promoter Score and renewal rate significantly exceed all competitors. A senior stakeholder insists the vision must shift to 'match every competitor feature within two quarters.' Applying evidence-based thinking, how should the Product Owner respond?

options.text: Publicly promise to match all competitor features by the deadline to placate the stakeholder, while privately continuing the current plan unchanged.

Share the retention and satisfaction evidence with the stakeholder, and propose evaluating competitive positioning based on the value actually delivered rather than committing to a feature-parity race before deciding whether to change the vision or backlog.
Dismiss the stakeholder's concern outright and make no attempt to explain the reasoning or share supporting data.
Comply immediately and commit the roadmap to feature parity because the stakeholder's seniority should override the Product Owner's own judgment.

explanation: High NPS and renewal despite lower feature count indicate the product's value proposition is resonating; a feature-parity race is an output-driven distraction that could divert investment from what's actually working. The evidence-based response is to share the data and jointly reassess positioning, not to simply obey, ignore, or fake compliance with the stakeholder.

question: After several increments testing a new feature direction, feedback is mixed: a small early-adopter segment is enthusiastic, but the broader customer base shows no engagement lift, and Ability to Innovate has decreased due to new technical debt. What is the most appropriate next step for the Product Owner before deciding whether to pivot, persevere, or stop?

options.text: Immediately double the investment because one segment is enthusiastic, disregarding the technical debt signal entirely.
Immediately pivot away from the new direction because overall engagement across the full customer base is flat.

Gather more targeted evidence to determine whether the enthusiastic segment represents a viable, sizable market or a narrow niche, and weigh that against the mounting cost to Ability to Innovate, before committing to a direction.
Continue the current direction for a fixed additional six months regardless of new evidence, because it was already committed to stakeholders.

explanation: Mixed signals — a narrow enthusiastic segment alongside flat broader engagement and rising technical debt — call for further targeted evidence-gathering rather than an immediate, unilateral pivot, escalation, or a fixed-timeline commitment. EBM's Ability to Innovate measure is a critical input that must be weighed alongside adoption evidence before deciding.

question: Market signals strongly suggest a pivot is warranted. Confident in the data, the Product Owner quietly redirects the Product Backlog toward the new direction over two Sprints without discussing it with key stakeholders or sharing the underlying evidence, reasoning that 'the PO owns the Product Backlog and doesn't need permission.' What is the primary risk with this approach, per Scrum Guide (2020) principles?

options.text: The primary risk is that Developers, not the Product Owner, technically own the Product Backlog under the Scrum Guide 2020, so redirecting it toward a pivot without their consent is an overreach of authority that the Developers could later reverse on their own.

While the Product Owner does have sole authority over Product Backlog content and ordering, the Scrum Guide expects that Backlog and its rationale to be visible and understood; bypassing stakeholders risks losing trust and causing misaligned execution, even when the pivot itself is evidence-based.

There is no risk at all, since the Scrum Guide 2020 gives the Product Owner sole authority over Product Backlog content and ordering with no expectation of transparency, so stakeholders need not see the new direction until the pivot shows up in a released Increment.

The primary risk is that any pivot requires prior approval from the Scrum Master before the Product Backlog can be changed; by skipping that approval step, the Product Owner breaks a change-control rule of the Scrum Guide 2020 and invalidates the Sprint Goals of the Sprints already planned with the Developers.

explanation: The Product Owner is indeed solely accountable for Product Backlog content and ordering, but that authority coexists with the expectation that the Backlog and the reasoning behind it remain transparent and understood by the Scrum Team and stakeholders. Making a significant, evidence-based pivot in secret risks eroding trust and causing misaligned execution, regardless of whether the underlying data was sound.

question: A senior VP repeatedly asks for private, ad hoc demos before every Sprint Review, bypassing the rest of the Scrum Team and stakeholders, so she can be 'first to know.' Which response is most consistent with the Scrum Guide (2020)?

options.text: Delegate the private demos to a Developer before each Sprint Review so the Product Owner can stay focused on Product Backlog refinement, while the VP still sees every Increment first and the rest of the stakeholders wait for the event.

Decline any contact with her outside formal Scrum events such as the Sprint Review, since Scrum confines Product Owner conversations with stakeholders to its events, so she has to wait for the Sprint Review like everyone else.

Explain that the Sprint Review is the collaborative event where the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the Increment together, invite her to attend and engage there, and offer another channel for general Product Goal updates if needed.

Agree to the private demo before each Sprint Review, since keeping a powerful stakeholder satisfied protects the roadmap's political support, and the Sprint Review itself still happens afterwards for the Scrum Team and the remaining stakeholders.

explanation: The Sprint Review exists precisely so the Scrum Team and stakeholders can inspect the outcome of the Sprint together and collaboratively determine next steps. Private ad hoc demos to a single stakeholder fragment that shared understanding and can create inconsistent expectations. The Product Owner's role is to channel stakeholder engagement into transparent, collective forums, not to grant special back-channel access.

question: A key enterprise customer demands a written commitment to exactly twelve named features by a fixed date six months out, threatening to cancel the contract otherwise. Which response best aligns with Scrum's empirical approach?

options.text: Sign the commitment as written, since large contracts require certainty, and direct the team to work overtime to guarantee the date.
Hand the negotiation entirely to the Scrum Master, since managing stakeholder conflict is a Scrum Master accountability rather than the Product Owner's.

Share the current empirical forecast based on team performance data, negotiate around the Product Goal, offer a forecast range for the highest-value items, and agree to revisit progress each Sprint so scope can adapt to new evidence.
Refuse to discuss any timelines at all, since Scrum prohibits date-based commitments and only the Sprint is a valid unit of planning.

explanation: EBM emphasizes using empirical evidence — such as historical velocity and forecast ranges — to have honest conversations about likely Time-to-Market rather than making speculative fixed commitments. Negotiating around outcomes and the Product Goal, with a cadence of re-forecasting each Sprint, protects both customer trust and the team's ability to adapt to new information.

question: Mid-Sprint, the Product Owner is running customer discovery interviews in parallel with the Development Team's work toward the current Sprint Goal (a checkout redesign). Early, limited signals suggest the current approach may not be optimal, but the evidence is not yet conclusive, and stakeholders expect the increment on schedule. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Immediately redirect the Development Team mid-Sprint to the new approach, since customer evidence should always override an existing Sprint plan.
Ask the Scrum Master to decide whether to change direction, since the Scrum Master is accountable for the effectiveness of the Scrum Team's practices.

Let the current Sprint continue toward its Sprint Goal, continue discovery in parallel, and use the resulting evidence to inform the ordering and content of future Product Backlog items and Sprint Goals.
Ignore the discovery findings entirely until the whole release finishes, so the Development Team's plan and stakeholder expectations remain undisturbed.

explanation: The Sprint Goal exists to give the Sprint coherence and focus, and Scrum does not expect the team to pivot on every early, inconclusive signal. The appropriate empirical response is to let the Sprint proceed, keep discovery running in parallel, and let stronger evidence shape upcoming Product Backlog ordering and future Sprint Goals — reserving Sprint cancellation for when the Sprint Goal is truly obsolete.

question: Two Scrum Teams share ownership of a single product used by both an internal operations business unit and an external customer segment. The operations leader insists their requests must always rank first because they 'fund the team,' while customer segment leads argue external revenue should always dominate. As the sole Product Owner for this product, what is the most defensible approach under Scrum?

options.text: Maintain two separate Product Backlogs, one per business unit, each with Product Owner authority delegated to the respective unit leader, and reconcile the two orderings at Sprint Planning so that the operations leader and the customer segment leads both keep control of their own priorities.

Give standing priority to whichever unit generates more direct revenue (the external customer segment today, the operations unit if its funding grows), since Current Value is defined strictly by revenue figures alone and revenue is the evidence EBM treats as most objective.

Alternate ordering between the two units' requests every other Sprint so influence remains balanced regardless of expected value, and explain the rotation transparently to both groups so that neither the operations leader nor the customer segment leads can claim any standing priority over the other group's requests.

Maintain a single ordered Product Backlog, order items by expected overall value toward the Product Goal using available evidence (such as expected impact on Current Value, Unrealized Value, and Time-to-Market), and transparently explain the rationale to both groups rather than granting either standing priority.

explanation: Scrum expects a single ordered Product Backlog managed by one accountable Product Owner, even when multiple business units compete for priority. EBM's Key Value Areas give the Product Owner an evidence-based, value-maximizing rationale to explain ordering decisions transparently, rather than defaulting to political leverage, rotation schemes, or an oversimplified single financial metric.

question: Midway through a Sprint, market conditions shift dramatically and the Sprint Goal becomes clearly obsolete; a major customer is demanding an entirely different feature set start immediately. What is the Scrum-consistent path forward?

options.text: The Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint because the Sprint Goal is obsolete, then works with the Scrum Team to plan a new Sprint with a Sprint Goal reflecting updated priorities.
The Scrum Master should cancel the Sprint, since they own the Scrum process and its events.
The Developers should unilaterally abandon the current Sprint Backlog and start the customer's new request without formally ending the Sprint.
The Scrum Team must complete the current Sprint regardless of the obsolete Sprint Goal, since only a Sprint's natural end can trigger replanning.

explanation: The Scrum Guide (2020) explicitly addresses this exact scenario: a Sprint can be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only the Product Owner holds the authority to do so. This preserves accountability while allowing the Scrum Team to replan around a Sprint Goal that reflects the new reality.

question: True or false? When multiple teams are working on the same product, their Sprints should start and end at the same time.

options.text: FALSE
TRUE

explanation:
According to Scrum.org, it's not mandatory to start and end the Sprints at the same time; e.g., most teams have four-week Sprints, but some of them have two-week Sprints.

question: Which THREE statements are correct about non-functional requirements?

options.text: They will be in the Sprint Backlog, but not the Product Backlog.
They can be incorporated right before the release.
Some of them can be controlled by the QA department of the organization.
They should be incorporated into every increment.
They will be considered in the Hardening Sprints.
Some of them can be added to the Product Backlog.
Some of them can be added to the Definition of Done.

explanation:
a. All items in the Sprint Backlog come from the Product Backlog, except for process improvement items that are generated in Sprint Retrospectives. b. Every Increment should be usable (potentially releasable), which means that everything that needs to be done is done. c. Remember that the team is cross-functional and does the work from A to Z. d. E.g., security: The way they can be "incorporated into every Sprint" is by adding them to the Definition of Done. e. There are no Hardening Sprints. f. E.g., something related to performance of a certain part of the software g. E.g., security, scalability, maintainability

question: When is user acceptance testing done?

options.text: In the Sprint Review meeting
At the end of the project
Before releases
During the Sprint

explanation:
* [PSM-12. Increment and Definition of Done](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/12/)

  We can't really call it "Done" while user acceptance tests (or any other tests) are not done. Therefore, it has to be done during the Sprint.

Some Agile approaches consider user acceptance testing for the review meeting at the end of the iteration, but that's not the case in Scrum -- at least according to the modern interpretations of Scrum.

question: Which TWO of the following may change during the Sprint?

options.text: Product Backlog
Sprint Backlog
Minimum level of quality
Product Goal

explanation:
a. The Product Backlog may change at any time. b. The tasks in the Sprint Backlog are always changing. Also, Scrum.org is not against changing the "items" in the Sprint Backlog either. c. The level of expected quality shouldn't decrease during the Sprint. d. The Product Goal is the long-term plan, and it doesn't change frequently, and certainly not in the middle of the Sprint. Those that stay fixed during the Sprint are needed to avoid distractions and create a more productive environment. After all, Sprints are not so long that they create problems.



* [PSM-05. Sprint](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/05/)

question: True or false? Besides the normal items that are about the features of the product, each Sprint Backlog may contain an item about improving the way we work.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE

explanation:
In the 2017 update of the Scrum Guide, a statement was added, saying that at least one high-priority process improvement item should be planned in each Sprint Retrospective and added to the next Sprint Backlog. The new version of the guide doesn't say that you have to do that, but it says that you can if you want. 



* [PSM-09. Sprint Retrospective](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/09/)

question: On average, items in the Sprint Backlog tend to be _____

options.text: the same size as those in the Product Backlog
smaller than those in the Product Backlog
larger than those in the Product Backlog

explanation:
This is how it works:
When you first add the items to the Product Backlog, you don't have to break them down into very small and clear items, because it's a form of upfront planning. Some of them may be very large. When you order the items, if they go on the top of the list, you have to make them clear, and make sure they can fit into one Sprint; therefore, you will break them down into smaller items. Some of those smaller items remain on the top, and some may go down. As a result, items at the top of the Product Backlog are on average smaller than those at the bottom. On the other hand, items in the Sprint Backlog come from the top of the Product Backlog, and therefore, we can say that the items in the Sprint Backlog are, on average, smaller than items in the Product Backlog.

question: Which of the following is NOT correct about Product Owners?

options.text: They measure the progress of the project.
They prioritize the work items in the Sprint Backlog.
They make the Product Backlog transparent and visible.
They measure progress toward the Product Goal.

explanation:
a. It's done by the Product Owner.
[PSM-08. Sprint Review](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/08/) b. Developers manage the Sprint Backlog. (For some decisions, they need to consult the Product Owner.)
[PSM-11. Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/11/) c. It's done by the Product Owner.
[PSM-15. Product Owner](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/15/), [PSM-10. Product Backlog and Product Goal](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/10/) d. It's done by the Product Owner.

question: True or false? Our velocity was 250 at the end of the 6th Sprint. It has become 275 at the end of the 8th Sprint. Therefore, we're creating more value now compared to before.

options.text: TRUE
FALSE

explanation: There's no direct relationship between velocity (speed) and value; e.g., maybe we're working faster on less valuable items, in which case, velocity will be higher, but value may be the same, higher, or lower. Many people consider velocity as the most important criterion, but that's not true -- we should rather be focused on value, Sprint Goal, and Product Goal.

question: True or false? There can be a maximum of one release per Sprint.

options.text: FALSE
TRUE

explanation:
* [PSM-12. Increment and Definition of Done](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/12/)

  As soon as an item is Done, a new Increment is created. Normally, multiple Increments are created during the Sprint, and all of them as usable (potentially releasable). If needed, some of them can be releases, without having to wait for the end of the Sprint.

question: At the end of the Sprint, all items are Done except for one that is almost Done. What should be done with this item?

options.text: Do not include it in the Increment.
It can be added to the Increment if the user acceptance tests are done.
Put it in the next Sprint Backlog.
The Sprint will be extended until we complete the item.

explanation:
a. Everything in the Increment must be Done -- i.e., 100% DONE! If an item is not done, we won't include it in the Increment and send it back to the Product Backlog. b. The Increment contains only 100% DONE items. c. It doesn't go to the next Sprint Backlog automatically. It has to go back to the Product Backlog and probably be re-estimated. Then the Product Owner may revise its contribution to value and change the ordering based on that. If the item is still at the top, it will be selected in the next Sprint Planning meeting. d. Sprints are timeboxed, meaning that we don't extend their duration. 

* [PSM-05. Sprint](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/05/)

question: True or false? When multiple teams are working on the same product, there should be one common Definition of Done that they all follow.

options.text: FALSE
TRUE

explanation:
* [PSM-12. Increment and Definition of Done](/online-courses/scrum-framework/lesson/12/)

  Teams don't create isolated Increments for themselves, but they integrate their work into the rest, and the Increments are always integrated and combined. In other words, Increments show the work of all teams. As a result, there should be a single Definition of Done for the product that all teams comply with, to make sure they can generate integrated Increments. If a team wants, they can have extra constraints in their Definition of Done (e.g., more tests), and that's fine, because when something complies with their definition, it will also comply with the overall definition.

question: Which TWO of the following are required by Scrum?

options.text: Sprint Retrospectives
Release planning
Definition of Ready
Definition of Done
Having full-time developers

explanation:
Everything in the Scrum Guide is required. Other concepts may be optional and acceptable, or unacceptable.
